recent_candidates.title: Democrats urge Rubio to act on Ethiopia
recent_candidates.author: Adrian Elimian
recent_candidates.excerpt: Democratic senators are urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to intervene diplomatically to address the crisis in Ethiopia, warning that renewed fighting in Tigray and escalating tensions with Eritrea could spiral into a multi-front war destabilizing the region. In a letter shared first with Semafor , lawmakers led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., the Senate Foreign Relations Committee’s top Democrat, asked the State Department to back an immediate ceasefire and new mediation including groups left out of the 2022 Pretoria Agreement. They also called for halting new arms sales to Ethiopia, reinstating Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopians in the US, and surging food aid as the fighting worsens the impact of drought on a deeply food insecure population. Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del. — expected to succeed the retiring Shaheen and chair the committee when Democrats take the Senate in January — also signed the letter, alongside the other three Democratic members of the committee’s Africa panel. “US diplomatic engagement has lacked the urgency, visibility, and coordination commensurate with the threat of another devastating civil war in Ethiopia and regional conflict,” the senators wrote. They warned against putting Eritrea’s Port of Assab — which Ethiopia wants to control — on the negotiating table. The State Department didn’t immediately return a request for comment. recent_candidates.title: IBM to curb sponsorship of visas, green cards
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: IBM said Tuesday it was discontinuing its sponsorship of US visas and green cards in its largest division, marking a win for the Trump administration, which has sought to crack down on corporations’ hiring of foreign workers. As part of its sweeping anti-immigration agenda, the White House has proposed changes including $100,000 filing fees for H-1B visas, which some critics have derided as a corporate tax on foreign talent . Following Republicans’ massive midterm defeat, US President Donald Trump has struck discordant notes on his immigration enforcement — conceding to that it had occasionally been “ too tough ,” but later walking back the comments after an outcry from his supporters, and promoting immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff. — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: Milei plots data center buildout in Patagonia
recent_candidates.author: Mary Lawrence Ware
recent_candidates.excerpt: Argentine President Javier Milei is pitching his country as a regulation-free “AI hub,” as US tech firms weigh building data centers abroad in the face of overwhelming domestic pushback. Milei, a self-described anarcho-capitalist , has pushed for a tax break for the facilities and touted Argentina’s “abundant energy” and “extensive, inhospitable land” as ideal for the rapid AI buildout. An energy executive planning a facility to power AI in rural Argentina told the Financial Times he was flooded with calls from potential US investors and clients, following midterm elections in which American voters resoundingly rejected data center construction: “[Argentina’s] coming late to the party, but it has huge potential to catch up .” — Mary Lawrence Ware

recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: Anthropic could generate $685 billion in revenue by 2030, placing it among the largest companies in the world, as the AI lab gears up for a $1.4 trillion IPO as soon as next week. The Goldman Sachs projection points to total sales of more than 130 times Anthropic’s 2025 figure, as the company gears up to spend about $900 billion on its AI buildout . The blockbuster sums will make CEO Dario Amodei one of the world’s most influential executives and, in turn, empower institutions sympathetic to his beliefs about effective altruism and existential risk, intensifying a debate over AI safety: The Trump administration has condemned effective altruism , and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang have criticized Amodei as a “doomer.” — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: US inflation slows less than expected in October
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: Hotter-than-expected US inflation data sparked a Treasury selloff Tuesday, heightening expectations of a rate increase at the Federal Reserve’s December meeting. Food prices saw a broad spike while a diesel crunch pushed up freight costs, widening out the number of affected goods categories. The price pressures are unlikely to be a one-month phenomenon, Santander’s chief US economist told The New York Times, as a simmering Iran war drives up the price of numerous commodities: “We run the risk that the floodgates open .” A Mizuho economist said the central bank could hike by half a point in response: “The Fed skipped October and now will probably need to do some make up .” — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: Huang scandal puts Nvidia chip loopholes in focus
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: The unfolding Nvidia saga has intensified scrutiny of the legal means by which top Chinese firms are able to access advanced American compute. While Megaspeed, the Singaporean firm at the center of the scandal, is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, Washington’s export controls have spawned lucrative opportunities for Asian cloud operators that get their hands on the most advanced Nvidia chips, offering a legal loophole to Chinese hyperscalers. Singapore-based DayOne is worth roughly $15 billion and counts ByteDance as its top customer, while Moonshot has looked to tap Nvidia chips hosted in Europe , highlighting “the nonsensical nature of our export control regime ,” a Carnegie Endowment expert said. “No administration has had the cojones to do something about it.” — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: Senate Republicans defeat push for delays, reelect Thune leader
recent_candidates.author: Burgess Everett
recent_candidates.excerpt: Senate Republicans voted today to proceed with their leadership elections, blowing past delay requests by a handful of members. The move paved the way for the reelection of current Republican leader John Thune, putting the rest of his team on the path to keep leading the conference in the next Congress. Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., a leader of the effort to delay, said the vote wasn’t particularly close and walked out in protest — but also underscored that his objection wasn’t about Thune, who he said has been “unfairly attacked” by the GOP base. “When you have this kind of defeat, you’d like to at least give people an opportunity to think about it,” Johnson said. But without a clear challenger to Thune, who won without opposition, most Republicans opted to vote against a period of purgatory after their electoral thrashing. — Burgess Everett

recent_candidates.title: Nvidia spy scandal tests whether any CEO is indispensable
recent_candidates.author: Liz Hoffman
recent_candidates.excerpt: Liz’s view How do you fire a CEO who has delivered 700,000% returns? One easy way is for the government to make you, but President Donald Trump thinks Nvidia’s Jensen Huang should keep his job. Another is for shareholders to make you, but I’d expect Nvidia’s shares to regain Monday’s losses — relatively muted by the standards of “our CEO had an affair with a Chinese spy” — by week’s end. Or at least I’d put better odds on that than the prediction markets are putting on Huang being fired, currently at 14% by the end of the year and a bit higher by the time Democrats get their gavel swinging. Much will depend on what those Democrats and Nvidia’s board, which is running its own investigation, unearth about who knew what and when. But the bigger question is what Nvidia is worth without Huang at its helm. Is he the indispensable force behind the world’s most valuable company, as Nvidia chronicler Stephen Witt suggested Monday, or an able salesman of a sought-after product that, by now, sells itself? Corporate chiefs today are more replaceable ( and replaced ) than ever, as the job has come to hinge more on handling constituencies of investors, regulators, and us in the media than on mastery of any particular corporate engine room. recent_candidates.author: Samuel Gregg
recent_candidates.excerpt: Slowly but surely, stagnation is stalking some of the world’s biggest economies. Whether it is low growth, astronomical public debt, inflationary pressures, unimpressive productivity, affordability issues, housing shortages, high energy prices, or weak levels of entrepreneurship, Western economies are far from healthy. Though specific events, like the wars in Iran and Ukraine, have contributed to these developments, many Western leaders persist in blaming their nations’ economic troubles on “neo-liberalism.” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, for example, has asserted that the economic policies associated with the Thatcher era are responsible for his country’s present challenges. Others recognize that the opposite of free markets—excessive government intervention—has contributed mightily to the economic problems facing Western countries. Back in 2024, former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi published an official European Union report that identified over-regulation and excessive bureaucracy as key to the economic sclerosis of many European nations. Alas, many such admissions are accompanied by the insistence that more state intervention is part of the solution. recent_candidates.author: George Hawley

recent_candidates.title: Labor Law’s Illiberal Trajectory
recent_candidates.author: Alex MacDonald
recent_candidates.excerpt: The Routledge Handbook of Classical Liberalism arrives at an odd moment. Published in July 2026, it trumpets a philosophy of personal liberty and free exchange to a public that increasingly seems to want less of both. On the political right, politicians clamor for higher tariffs and tighter restrictions on immigration. And on the left, they call for new taxes on wealth. The Handbook ’s authors respond to these calls with the academic equivalent of a battle cry—660 pages of thorough scholarship and reasoned argument, each one urging that classical-liberal ideas are still relevant. From trade policy to public health, they say, society is still served best by a mix of strong property rights, clear rules of law, and a commitment to personal choice. The book is a free-market credo doubling as a doorstop. But thorough as the book is, it is notable for what it omits. Over thirty-eight chapters, it spares not one word for modern labor policy. And that choice is, depressingly, hard to fault. In all of modern public policy, labor policy may have become the least welcoming to liberal ideas. Debates over labor policy today almost never focus on property rights, free exchange, or other liberal values. Instead, the debates center on ideas like “ interest arbitration ,” a system where contracts are replaced by arbitral awards, and “ co-regulation ,” which replaces private bargaining with centralized regulation. These proposals don’t even pretend to promote free markets or individual choice.

recent_candidates.title: 'Junk history' and Swedish neutrality
recent_candidates.author: Johan Wennstrom
recent_candidates.excerpt: The historian Stephen Kotkin of Stanford’s Hoover Institution has penned an important new essay on the phenomenon of “junk history”: reductionist or plainly wrong interpretations of historical events that have little or no basis in empirical reality but are nevertheless “marshaled in policy debates as justification for action, up to launching wars.” The emblematic example, which has recently been used by advocates for the war with Iran, is the failure of British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain to truly ensure “peace in our time” at Munich in 1938. As Kotkin once put it, “It turns out not everything is Munich. It turns out Munich wasn’t even Munich when you get down into the nitty-gritty details.” Another example of junk history is what many otherwise well-informed American observers think they know about Sweden’s conduct during World War II and the Cold War. recent_candidates.author: Dan M. Ford
recent_candidates.excerpt: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). This decision comes down to issues that have little to do with the act itself, nor even really with trade between the United States and these countries. Rather, in both cases, their removal from AGOA serves as an act of retribution from a president unhappy with their governments’ policies on domestic or regional issues. But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. The preferential trade agreement — originally signed into law in 2000 by President Bill Clinton and most recently renewed in September for two additional years — provides duty-free access for over 7,000 goods to the U.S. market for qualifying sub-Saharan countries. In exchange for this preferential access, AGOA requires countries to meet a set of vague requirements, including reducing barriers to American exporters, ensuring governance and human rights standards, and not posing a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. The U.S. president has unilateral authority to designate a country ineligible for AGOA benefits under these standards. Industry and policymakers have long advocated for regulatory harmonization and should continue to push for smarter regulations that actually reduce cyber risk. Yet it has never been less important to ensure those regulations are harmonized. AI can reduce the “harmonization tax,” the cost of addressing compliance tasks that can overwhelm companies for little actual improvement in security or reduced risk. In her new book, Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American Right , Stephanie Slade, a writer for the libertarian journal Reason , argues that a flourishing society requires a shared commitment to both liberty and virtue. She contends that the conservative movement in the 20th century at its best was devoted to both of these ideals—to the protection of personal, political, and economic freedom and to the fostering and encouragement of moral goodness in the culture. recent_candidates.title: China’s marriage rate drops to lowest level in almost two decades
recent_candidates.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
recent_candidates.excerpt: China’s marriage rate fell to its lowest level in almost two decades , adding to worries about the country’s demographic crisis. Data this week showed 4.65 million couples tied the knot from January through September, while 2.08 million couples got divorced. Beijing has in recent years rolled out a series of measures aimed at increasing marriage rates and childbearing. But while some regions have seen results from such policies, fertility rates for the country as a whole continue to plummet, with women on average having fewer children than even during the era of the one-child policy . The demographic shift will have huge fiscal consequences for decades to come, with one prominent China academic urging Beijing to “formulate forward-looking plans for immigration .” — Jeronimo Gonzalez

recent_candidates.title: Top Democrat vows to increase oversight of intelligence agencies
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: The top Democrat in charge of overseeing US intelligence agencies in the next Congress vowed Wednesday to increase oversight of the Trump administration’s expanded use of covert action. The White House has reportedly increased spy agencies’ footprint in Mexico and Latin America, and against adversaries in cyberspace , while also firing hundreds of longtime officials. Rep. Jim Himes said the investigations would probe whether officials “were fired because they said something that was inconsistent with what the president wanted to be true .” Congress is also looking to scrutinize a rash of 11 or more suicides this year at US cyber agencies, where workload has surged in the past year in response to escalating foreign conflicts, Bloomberg reported. — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: Nvidia CEO scandal exposes gaps in US chip controls
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: A Chinese university with ties to the country’s military was able to obtain Nvidia’s most powerful chips last month despite being on a US blacklist, Reuters reported, as scrutiny over the chipmaker reveals holes in Washington’s regulatory framework. The disclosure comes as lawmakers press the Trump administration on its investigation into Megaspeed, the Singapore firm at the center of the Jensen Huang spy scandal, amid reports that the Commerce Department has delayed efforts to blacklist the company suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. US restrictions have accelerated Beijing’s efforts to develop homegrown semiconductors — independence that will allow it “to scale faster than the US,” Semafor’s tech editor argued: Nvidia, crucial to the US’ advantage, will be “ fundamentally weakened ” without Huang. — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: CoreWeave results drive broad tech rally
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: US tech stocks surged Wednesday following stronger-than-expected CoreWeave earnings, as the AI trade recovered after last week’s selloff. Despite the company’s massive borrowing, investors were encouraged by CoreWeave beating revenue expectations and raising its forecast, as traders parsed the key Anthropic vendor’s results for clues ahead of the AI firm’s planned IPO next week. CoreWeave shares, though, are down 20% so far this year , and the company is not throwing enough cash off its business to cover its roughly $41 billion of net debt, amid jitters over the sustainability of the AI buildout. Still, “a healthier-looking CoreWeave today at least provides some reassurance to the broader AI market and especially to Anthropic,” a Bloomberg columnist wrote. — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: Klobuchar successor talk centers on second-term House member
recent_candidates.author: Burgess Everett
recent_candidates.excerpt: Democrats are starting to debate who will succeed Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., when she’s sworn in as governor next year. There’s one name that keeps coming up: Democratic Rep. Kelly Morrison, who just won her second term to the House and served in the state legislature before that. Klobuchar hasn’t made a final decision on the pick, according to a person familiar with her thinking. But many Democrats believe Morrison is a frontrunner after she passed on the 2026 Senate race. Asked if she wants the appointment, Morrison said only that she’s “excited” about Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan and about representing her district: “The governor-elect will appoint someone, and I know she’ll be right by the people of Minnesota.” Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., who lost the Senate primary to Flanagan, is seen as a longshot for the appointment.

recent_candidates.title: Omar wants to get back on House Foreign Affairs Committee
recent_candidates.author: Nicholas Wu
recent_candidates.excerpt: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., wants to get back on the House Foreign Affairs Committee after Republicans removed her, though she’s also angling for a spot on the Appropriations panel. “I would love to,” she told Semafor of Foreign Affairs. “That is my favorite committee. ... I’m thinking of Approps and other committees, so we’ll see how it all shakes out.” If she were to return to the Foreign Affairs Committee, she could lead its Africa subpanel because of her seniority. The subcommittee’s current top Democrat, Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., said “it’s still being figured out.” But Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the committee’s top Democrat, said it’s Omar’s “choice” whether to chair the Africa subpanel. House Democrats will soon start the process of populating committees, and with a larger-than-expected House majority, they’ll face some tough decisions about divvying up spots, especially on sought-after panels.

recent_candidates.title: West Wing reshuffles as Miller settles in
recent_candidates.author: Shelby Talcott
recent_candidates.excerpt: More changes are expected across the White House in the coming weeks as Stephen Miller settles into his new role as chief of staff, with some aides who worked closely with Susie Wiles shifting into new roles. A White House official told Semafor that Meghan Bauer, who heads the Office of Cabinet Affairs, will shift to a different role in the White House. (Multiple other sources, however, suggested to Semafor that Bauer is expected to depart in the coming weeks.) Meanwhile, Walker Barrett, a senior policy adviser to Wiles, will move under the deputy chief of staff for policy, the official said. The staffing changes offer an early glimpse of how the West Wing is reshuffling as Trump and Miller reshape the team post-midterms. It remains unclear how many more aides will change assignments or depart ahead of the new year.

recent_candidates.title: Local media startup City Cast reshuffles leadership
recent_candidates.author: Max Tani
recent_candidates.excerpt: The locally-focused media startup City Cast has named Andi McDaniel, the company’s chief creative officer, its new CEO, replacing David Plotz. City Cast launched in 2021 as a local podcast and newsletter venture aimed at serving cities where local news was shifting from old newspapers and radio to screens. The company has since expanded to 13 cities, including Austin, Las Vegas, and Philadelphia, among others. “This next chapter for us is about expanding audiences. It’s about adapting to AI, and it’s about making the business successful,” McDaniel, a veteran public radio executive and co-founder of City Cast , told Semafor. City Cast has gained greater visibility in recent months, primarily for its expansion in its hometown. As Semafor first noted last year, in response to what the company saw as an opportunity created by the turbulence at The Washington Post, City Cast scaled up its newsroom and business in Washington. City Cast is backed by Graham Holdings, which owned the Post before selling to Jeff Bezos. City Cast DC now has 20 people on staff, and said it has found some success attracting a younger audience to its content, tripling the size of people it reaches regularly from roughly 100,000 at the beginning of the year to around 300,000. Not every bet has paid off. The company shuttered two arms, in Boise and Houston. recent_candidates.title: Airwallex’s CEO isn't worried about AI
recent_candidates.author: Reed Albergotti
recent_candidates.excerpt: Jack Zhang isn’t worried about AI taking over global finance, but he is concerned about cybersecurity. Zhang co-founded Australian fintech unicorn Airwallex, which allows businesses to make cross-border payments and manage finances in dozens of countries, and is now morphing into an agentic finance company. Zhang joined Future Proof to discuss how his company is using AI to build systems to help companies handle their finances — essentially building an AI-managed CFO office. The company currently relies mainly on ChatGPT and Claude, but Zhang also said it’s looking at developing proprietary models using open-weight solutions. Zhang doesn’t think AI will get so good that it can entirely replace humans, at least not in his field. “The laws still require you to have somebody sign off as auditor, and how the auditor does that sign-off can be assisted by agents,” he said. “I don’t think we can completely get rid of the human in the loop.” What Zhang is “very, very, very, very worried” about is cybersecurity. With news about cyber breaches emerging almost daily, the company is tackling the issue by using behavioral monitoring and hiring experts from the Australian Department of Defence and Palantir, among other strategies. “We’re moving hundreds of billions of dollars today ... We’re constantly paranoid about how good our defense [is] against this type of threat,” he said. — Reed Albergotti

recent_candidates.title: Nvidia is more than a chip company
recent_candidates.author: Reed Albergotti
recent_candidates.excerpt: Reed’s view Nvidia has been battered over the past couple of days, but it could get worse. That is, if founder and CEO Jensen Huang is forced or chooses to step down, or if investigations pin him down for doing something illegal. In most sectors of the economy, CEOs are expected to run businesses well, but they are generally interchangeable parts — albeit expensive ones. Google and Apple show that founder CEOs, which are harder to replicate, can be replaced. But even among founder CEOs, Huang stands apart for bold bets that helped him endure short-term suffering in return for long-term gain. Most people know Nvidia for the climbing stock in their portfolios, or the GPUs on every tech company’s Christmas list. But his creation of the CUDA platform in 2006 is perhaps the best example of how he’s been able to step ahead of the industry for decades. Nvidia’s computing platform and programming model, the software that essentially underpins the modern AI industry, created one of the most valuable moats in business history. A half dozen years later, seeing the progress in neural networks, he pivoted to AI. Huang realized AI would require massive data centers with interconnected chips, and concluded that networking would become the bottleneck. He bet billions on the development of NVLink, a nervous system that allows discrete GPUs to act as one massive supercomputer, and the $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox Technologies, the Israeli networking company, in 2019. recent_candidates.title: Progressives try to have it both ways on Medicare for All
recent_candidates.author: Nicholas Wu
recent_candidates.excerpt: The News Progressive Democrats are trying a tricky feat as their party takes power : endorsing Medicare for All while quietly pushing for smaller steps toward it. Their dilemma began with the party’s remarkable midterm success. Democrats are united in attributing their electoral triumph in part to voter backlash against GOP healthcare moves — and this year, even purple-district candidates won while backing Medicare for All. But now, the left is split on how to make it happen. Without a filibuster or veto-proof majority in Congress next year, Democrats are calibrating their expectations for change based on what can potentially pass through the maneuver known as reconciliation, which requires only a simple majority. Some progressives are calling for a unified drive to lower the Medicare eligibility age, add guaranteed coverage up to age 19, and add dental and vision coverage. That could offer a middle ground for party leaders who are looking to stave off fights over bills likely to be vetoed by President Donald Trump. Embracing a big step toward pure Medicare for All could also hand a victory to progressives who have long pushed for legislative action — if they can settle for something less than the litmus test they set up. “It’s the perfect way for us to get ready for the next trifecta if we pass those three bills, and then if we mark up the entire Medicare for All bill,” said Rep. recent_candidates.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom to Senate in massive upset
recent_candidates.author: By Jason Beeferman
recent_candidates.excerpt: Mississippi voted blue, in a shock win for Democrats. Democrat Scott Colom ousted Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that went for President Donald Trump by 23 points in 2024. He will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era — and the first Democrat from the state headed to the Senate in 44 years. Colom, a Democratic district attorney, ran a scrappy campaign that saw some national money and resources in the final stretch of the race. Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and had since won election to the seat twice, but she faced attacks from Colom that she was out of touch and indifferent to rising grocery and gas prices during Trump’s second term. National Democratic groups hadn't paid much attention to the Mississippi Senate race until an October surge of excitement for Colom drew late spending and attention. Colom's win is a boost to the Democratic Party as it seeks to gain a larger foothold in the South and improve their standing with Black voters. It’s also a major vindication for Colom and other Southern Democrats who argued Mississippi had been neglected for far too long.

recent_candidates.title: Biden says he wouldn't have run in 2024 if he knew about his cancer
recent_candidates.author: By Gregory Svirnovskiy
recent_candidates.excerpt: Former President Joe Biden would not have run for reelection in 2024 if he had known about his cancer, he said in an interview released Wednesday in which he also sought to downplay the historic debate performance that helped end his political career. "If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have not gone forward because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running," he said in the interview with People magazine , which was conducted last week following Democrats’ big midterm wins and ahead of his upcoming memoir’s release. The former president announced his diagnosis — Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer — in May 2025, just four months after leaving the White House. It triggered an outpouring of public support — but it also raised questions about how doctors failed to catch the cancer earlier and whether it might have contributed to Biden’s apparent decline toward the end of his term. “I think it’s very sad, actually. I’m surprised that it wasn’t, you know, the public wasn’t notified a long time ago because to get to [a Gleason score of] 9, that’s a long time,” President Donald Trump told reporters shortly after Biden’s announcement. Prior to his diagnosis, Biden hadn’t been screened for prostate cancer since 2014 . U.S. guidelines have long recommended that men shouldn't be screened for the cancer once they hit their 70s. recent_candidates.excerpt: When Annie Andrews announced her longshot campaign for U.S. Senate last May, the Democrat from South Carolina pitched herself as a “busy mom.” “Lindsey [Graham] is going to tell you I am radical, that I am crazy,” Andrews said in her launch video . “But here’s the thing: I am literally a busy mom and a pediatrician who plays peek-a-boo with my patients, watches Bluey with my kids … and spends most of my free time shuttling them to dance, Tae Kwon Do and football.” Now, she is one of a record number of women who will serve in the next Congress. And as a 46-year-old mother of three school-aged children, she’s among several Democratic women who flipped seats and governor’s mansions this November with campaign messages centered on parenting and affordability. recent_candidates.title: The Great False Binary
recent_candidates.author: David D. Corey

recent_candidates.title: To Preserve Collegiate Competition, Constrain It
recent_candidates.author: Asheesh Agarwal
recent_candidates.excerpt: To paraphrase an infamous paradox, can the government create a competitive regime so dysfunctional that even the government can’t save it? Due to a mishmash of litigation and legislation, as well as $21 billion in revenue , today’s college sports landscape resembles neither an academic paradise nor a capitalist utopia, but rather Thomas Hobbes’s war of all against all. Every “student-athlete” becomes a free agent every year. Schools change conferences heedless of geographic or historical ties. One state allows pro athletes to play college ball while many schools lose tens of millions annually on their athletic departments. Football and men’s basketball, the revenue sports, effectively subsidize the Olympic and women’s sports, yet Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) dollars may soon bring this model to an end. Against this backdrop, the best way to preserve competition in college athletics may be, in fact, to limit it. As Neal McCluskey suggests in his forum lead , a limited antitrust exemption would allow the NCAA to create a sustainable competitive landscape in which numerous schools could continue to compete in the revenue sports, schools would have incentives to support nonrevenue sports, and student-athletes could profit off their athletic ability. recent_candidates.author: Rebecca Burgess
recent_candidates.excerpt: Editor’s note: This essay was originally published on May 25, 2026. Crisp against the gloaming, a bugle sounds a rising then falling strain. It’s 5 pm. It’s cold. Yet in the nation’s capital, something embers. While DC’s iPhone-occupied evening toilers and travelers scurry about to their next diversion, the lone uniformed Doughboy standing at 1400 Pennsylvania Avenue signals a time-honored but incongruous musical thought of reflection for day’s ending. My feet or my heart or my head have drawn me back here again, to the inscribed words, the murmuring water splatting, and the parading in bronze—of the human, and of the nation—that all together make up America’s newest national monument, the National World War I Memorial, at Pershing Park . Alongside its American precursor, the French version of “Taps,” la sonnerie “Aux Morts,” was sounded. recent_candidates.title: Tech CEOs circle wagons around Huang despite China spy claims
recent_candidates.author: Margaux Maccoll
recent_candidates.excerpt: Billionaire Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, who is currently holding the entire U.S. economy on his leather jacket-wearing back, has allegedly been canoodling with an AI executive-turned-Chinese spy. You might expect this news to terrify Silicon Valley, the home of the new age defense contractors. You might expect calls for Huang's head. The tepid reaction shows a splintering of the tech-China hawk movement. Moguls in this space have spent the last few years spreading fear over China’s potential AI dominance — in part because of a belief in American exceptionalism, but also out of fierce self-interest. But what happens now that one of their own has potentially threatened said AI dominance? “Saving Jensen is right now the cause in the VC world,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. Up until last month, Huang was the platonic ideal of a tech founder. recent_candidates.title: Iran War Day 257: Iran Threatens U.S. Bases in Europe
recent_candidates.author: Luke Nicastro
recent_candidates.excerpt: Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Wednesday Iran would strike U.S. bases in Europe if they were used to launch attacks. “If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well,” Rezaei told a Lebanese outlet in an interview. The statement is the most explicit threat yet issued against U.S. installations outside the Middle East. Separately, an Iranian news agency also quoted Rezaei as saying that Iran “will not remove even a single particle of enriched nuclear material from the country.” Also on Wednesday, the insurer Allianz said in a report the Iran War would likely cost Gulf countries more than $200 billion in damage to physical infrastructure. Factoring in other economic effects, like tourism and trade impacts, the report put the total cost of the war at around $790 billion through 2030. Oil prices have remained below recent highs: Brent crude opened around $92 per barrel, and AAA reports that the average price of regular gasoline in the United States is $3.94 per gallon. recent_candidates.title: Jim Jordan Elected New House GOP Leader
recent_candidates.author: Luke Nicastro
recent_candidates.excerpt: House Republicans chose Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) to be their next leader in a closed-door meeting Tuesday. Jordan, a founder of the Freedom Caucus and close ally of President Donald Trump, beat out Rep. Steve Scalise (R-LA) in a 106-73 vote. As House Majority Leader, Scalise had worked closely with outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA); Jordan’s victory is widely seen as signalling a break with Johnson’s leadership. Following Republicans’ disastrous showing in last week’s midterm elections, Jordan will lead his party as it enters the minority come January. recent_candidates.author: James P. Pinkerton

recent_candidates.title: Nueve policías heridos durante la huelga en Madrid
recent_candidates.author: THE OBJECTIVE
recent_candidates.excerpt: Nueve policías han resultado heridos este miércoles en Madrid en los disturbios con manifestantes y enfrentamientos con piquetes ocurridos a lo largo de la jornada de huelga general , según fuentes policiales. Cinco de los agentes fueron heridos por contusiones en los disturbios ocurridos por la noche al final de la manifestación de Madrid, en los que han sido detenidas cuatro personas. Estos agentes han resultado contusionados por lanzamientos de piedras y objetos contundentes de los manifestantes, mientras que los otros cuatro policías heridos a lo largo de la jornada de huelga lo fueron en distintos choques entre piquetes y trabajadores. En los disturbios ocurridos esta noche al término de la marcha que ha recorrido parte del centro de la capital, como colofón de la huelga, la Policía ha cargado contra un grupo de manifestantes y ha detenido a cuatro personas por desórdenes y atentado a la autoridad. Otras dos personas han sido sancionadas en aplicación de la Ley de Seguridad Ciudadana. La huelga general deja más de 100 detenidos, la mitad de ellos en Barcelona THE OBJECTIVE Debido a la gravedad de las agresiones, los agentes emplearon espray lacrimógeno y material antidisturbios. A lo largo de toda la jornada, las Unidades de Intervención Policial (UIP) han detenido a ocho personas e identificado a 842. recent_candidates.title: Bruselas alerta de los ciberataques a las islas de congelados en los supermercados de la UE
recent_candidates.author: THE OBJECTIVE
recent_candidates.excerpt: La Comisión Europea ha advertido este miércoles de los ciberataques a los supermercados europeos. Los sistemas de refrigeración han sido los primeros objetivos y deben servir como una «llamada de atención» sobre la vulnerabilidad de las infraestructuras críticas de la Unión. Por ello, recoge Europa Press, reclama a los Veintisiete que refuercen las medidas de protección para evitar que este tipo de incidentes se repitan en el futuro. La correcta conservación de los alimentos es crucial. «Aunque los ataques no han provocado consecuencias significativas para la seguridad alimentaria ni para la salud pública, deberían servir como una llamada de atención para todos», ha subrayado la vicepresidenta ejecutiva de la Comisión para la Soberanía Tecnológica, Henna Virkkunen, que apunta a que la UE «no puede permitirse mantener dependencias o debilidades estratégicas» que expongan sus infraestructuras críticas «a riesgos inaceptables». Estas infraestructuras «son cada vez más importantes» para garantizar una conectividad «fiable y ultrarrápida», así como el intercambio de datos e información, la detección de drones y la coordinación operativa en tiempo real, ha recordado la finesa Virkkunen. En este sentido, la vicepresidenta ha reclamado acelerar la retirada de los proveedores considerados «de alto riesgo», como las tecnológicas chinas Huawei o ZTE , al considerar que los Veintisiete deben actuar con mayor determinación para reducir sus dependencias tecnológicas de terceros países. recent_candidates.excerpt: España lleva tiempo acumulando razones de sobra para una huelga general : apagones, trenes que descarrilan o colisionan causando decenas de muertos, corrupción, invasiones territoriales, una inmigración masiva que depaupera los servicios públicos, la precarización de los salarios, la presión fiscal unida a la pérdida de poder adquisitivo o la imposibilidad del acceso a la vivienda. Sin embargo, durante ocho años los sindicatos de clase han estado callados como tumbas. Hasta este miércoles, justo a las puertas de las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre. UGT y CCOO han celebrado este miércoles una huelga general que, desde el primer momento, ha sido un despropósito. Una auténtica burla en la cara de los trabajadores. La escasa movilización de los sindicatos ha terminado dando paso a una jornada de tensión en la que los piquetes han tratado de imponer por la fuerza el seguimiento del paro, han provocado el cierre de comercios y han terminado enfrentándose a la Policía Nacional. Una huelga general debería ser el último recurso de los trabajadores frente a una situación de gravedad excepcional, no un instrumento al servicio de una estrategia política.
